name: Aaron Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What do you do on a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, have an MBA and lead six analysts in sales operations for a large company. By nine I'm checking the renewal forecast, then I settle disputes between sales and finance about what can count as a booked order. I use AI daily for draft notes and patterns, but the best part is calling someone and finding the one fact the screen missed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is going on at home alongside that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner teaches, and we rent while building a deposit for a flat. We have about three months of expenses saved, my pay is ordinary for this job, and there are a few comparable roles nearby. My bonus changes year to year, so I won't treat it like rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the sales operations team we should use the drafting tool for the weekly forecast and stop pretending copying figures is a badge of honor. The client calls and deciding which promise we can keep still belong to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like a better tool and I already use AI every day to prepare my review notes. Still, my partner and I have only about three months of expenses saved, and a bonus miss would slow the deposit we want for a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll keep the AI forecast draft, compare it with actual orders, and have my six analysts flag anything the tool invents. In the first year of this plateau, I'll continue our 180 monthly deposit transfer and ask for a better bonus formula at my next review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about keeping the job and a little impatient with slow decisions. Small AI gains are welcome if we actually use the time we get back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is one thing the tool invents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It once treated an unsigned renewal as booked revenue, because the email sounded cheerful. I caught it by calling the account owner before the forecast went to finance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask about the bonus formula now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My bonus rewards forecast speed but not the bad commitments we prevent. I'd rather be paid for a clean order book than a bright slide.

say: I'd use **AI drafts** for the forecast and spend less time copying numbers.
I'd keep **client calls** and promises people can answer for.
think: Daily AI use makes my **work quicker**, but a missed bonus would slow our flat deposit.
Three months saved gives us room, though I don't want **bad orders** to hide in a bright forecast.
do: Compare the **AI forecast** with signed orders and have six analysts flag invented figures.
Transfer **180 monthly** to the deposit account and request a bonus review this year.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and impatient with wasted time.
S0.quote: I'd rather be paid for a clean order book than a bright slide.
fieldNote: He is an **early user** who still checks whether renewals are actually signed.
His bonus concern is **specific**, tied to the quality of orders rather than the speed of a forecast.

steps.text: Check each AI sales forecast against signed orders
Transfer 180 monthly into the flat deposit account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say Steady Disruption will make routine forecasts and customer replies cheap, and our company should turn that time into better account work. I'd volunteer to build the first dashboard, provided the team can see and correct its mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could win a bigger role by making the system work, but I could also make half my analysts unnecessary. I am not going to claim the company will keep six seats just because I ask politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll build a pilot dashboard with two account teams, track wrong renewal dates, and teach my six analysts how to check the output. In the first year of disruption, I'd propose a client-risk role for myself and ask the director to place displaced analysts into account support where vacancies exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel energized and worried at the same time. If the pilot works, I will have helped the company ask why it needs our present team size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you tell the analysts about that risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them the headcount math before I ask them to help build the dashboard. My younger brother took an apprenticeship at a small firm; he taught me that a person deserves to know what work will still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if account support has no vacancies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I won't describe it as a placement plan. I'd ask the director for a funded training offer and clear notice, and I would help each analyst put the work they did on a real application.

say: I'd build a **pilot dashboard** and let staff correct errors before wider use.
I'd say freed time should become **account work**, with vacancy checks for anyone displaced.
think: A successful tool could bring me a **bigger role** while shrinking my six-person team.
I cannot promise **six seats** will remain after routine forecasts get cheaper.
do: Pilot the **dashboard** with two account teams and track wrong renewal dates this month.
Teach **six analysts** to check its output; seek client-risk work and real placements in the first year.
feel: I feel **energized and worried** about improving a tool that may shrink my team.
S1.quote: If the pilot works, I will have helped the company ask why it needs our present team size.
fieldNote: His ambition and guilt meet in the **same pilot**, making his public pitch more careful.
He refuses to call account support a **placement route** without vacancies and asks for funded training otherwise.

steps.text: Pilot a renewal dashboard with two account teams this month
Propose a client-risk role if forecast management shrinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team AGI by 2028 can do our forecasts and most account planning, so the staffing decision must be made in the open. I would offer to test the system, but I would ask for written terms before anyone trains it on client records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the quick one that scares me: my value is mostly thinking, and robots arriving around 2031 don't protect a sales operations manager in 2028. Three months saved and my partner's steady teaching pay would buy time, but I might lose both my role and bonus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll stop counting the bonus in our flat budget and ask the director for the AGI trial's access rules and staffing dates. In the first year after 2028, I'd test AGI on old forecasts with consent and compare errors; if my post is removed, I'd apply for account manager roles at the two other large firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, although I can still make a plan. I don't want to be the person who built a system with client data and learned the rules only when the cuts came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would hold the flat deposit in cash and postpone viewings until we know whether my salary remains. We could live on teaching pay for a stretch, but not keep saving at the same rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What written term matters most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want a date for staffing decisions and a line saying who can see client records in the trial. I would rather delay a clever pilot than expose a client's figures without permission.

say: I'd ask for **open staffing dates** and written client-data rules before testing AGI.
I'd tell analysts **forecasts and account plans** change in 2028, before robots arrive.
think: My **thinking work** is exposed in 2028; the later robot date offers no shelter.
Three months saved and teaching pay buy time, but losing my **bonus and role** would delay our flat.
do: Remove the **bonus** from our flat budget and request trial access rules now.
After 2028, test **old forecasts** with consent; seek account manager roles if my post disappears.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, with a plan but little time to protect pay and client trust.
S2.quote: I would rather delay a clever pilot than expose a client's figures without permission.
fieldNote: He welcomes AGI testing only after **client permissions** and staffing terms are clear.
The household can lean on **teaching pay**, yet a role and bonus loss would halt flat viewings.

steps.text: Postpone flat viewings until his salary outlook is clear
Test AGI against old forecasts with client consent after 2028
Apply for account manager roles at two nearby firms if cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team AGI by 2031 gives us time to move from producing forecasts to negotiating promises with clients. I'd ask directors to publish how many account roles they expect, not just offer a course with no vacancy behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let me build a genuine client book, and my MBA plus current sales experience would help. The software still reaches analysis and planning in 2031; waiting for robots around 2034 would be a mistake for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next quarter, I'll ask to shadow two account managers on renewal calls and take a paid negotiation course if the company offers one. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd seek an account lead vacancy if one exists; if there is none, I'd approach nearby firms with the renewal cases I handled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than alarmed. Five years lets me prove I can close a difficult renewal, but I need the openings to be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on those calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn where the account manager refuses a discount and what they offer instead. I can produce a clean risk chart already; I need to hear how a client decides to stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want a vacancy count. Would you leave if it is small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building my book while I interview outside, not wait for a promise from our director. My partner and I can absorb some travel, but I won't move home on the chance of an offer.

say: I'd ask directors for **account vacancy counts**, not only training offers.
I'd tell analysts to build **client negotiation** experience before 2031.
think: Five years could give me a **client book** that matters beyond forecast production.
My planning work changes in **2031**, not when robots reach hands-on tasks around 2034.
do: Shadow **two account managers** next quarter; take negotiation training if the company pays.
Seek an **account lead vacancy** after 2031, then nearby employers if none exists.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with time to gain experience if real openings exist.
S3.quote: I can produce a clean risk chart already; I need to hear how a client decides to stay.
fieldNote: He uses the longer runway to gain **client-call experience**, outside the forecasts AI can produce.
His willingness to move roles depends on **vacancies**, not a certificate or director's promise.

steps.text: Shadow two account managers on renewal calls next quarter
Apply for an account lead vacancy after 2031 if one exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our younger analysts AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to build relationships and judgment alongside stronger tools. I'd push the company to let junior staff join real client calls rather than become caretakers of a forecast screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 when thinking AI arrives; I could already be running accounts by then. My fear is getting a comfortable title for ten years while the actual client trust sits elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep using AI for draft forecasts and ask for a monthly client visit with an account manager. If one agrees, I'll join the visits and learn how a renewal is negotiated. Over the decade I'd build a record of renewals I helped close; in the first year after 2036, I'd stay if I own real client relationships and look outside if my job is only checking a system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about my own choices, though the team needs the same chance to learn. Ten years should be enough to move if I don't waste them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the flat during that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if our deposit and emergency savings are separate and my partner's teaching work stays steady. I won't ask my partner to put a home on hold for a date a decade away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a real client relationship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A client would call me about a missed delivery before sending a formal complaint. If my name is only on a dashboard, the client relationship belongs to someone else.

say: I'd ask for **junior client calls** as part of the decade of preparation.
I'd say **relationships and judgment** deserve practice alongside stronger tools.
think: At **37**, I could be running accounts rather than tending a forecast screen.
A comfortable title could hide a lack of **client trust** and leave my role exposed.
do: Keep using **AI forecast drafts**; join monthly client visits if an account manager agrees.
Build a **renewal record** before 2036; stay for real accounts or seek another job afterward.
feel: I feel **fairly calm** about personal choices, while concerned for junior staff.
S4.quote: If my name is only on a dashboard, the client relationship belongs to someone else.
fieldNote: He sees the long runway as a way to **earn client trust**, not simply collect a new title.
His flat purchase stays **conditional** on separate emergency savings and his partner's steady teaching work.

steps.text: Keep checking AI forecast drafts against signed renewals this year
Join monthly client visits to learn negotiation if an account manager agrees
Apply for outside account work after 2036 if role becomes system checking

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the company could replace our forecast work before any of us has built a client book. Clear staffing dates, consent rules for client data, and actual account vacancies would help me prepare and tell my team the truth.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is allowed to use the clients' figures to train the new system. I won't ask my analysts to break a client's trust just to win a pilot.

headlineQuote: I won't ask my analysts to break a client's trust just to win a pilot.
portrait: At **27**, Aaron leads six sales operations analysts and uses AI every day to draft and check forecasts.
He and his teacher partner have **three months saved**; fast AGI makes them exclude his variable bonus from flat plans.
He eagerly builds **new tools**, while insisting on client consent, error checks and honest staffing numbers.
Fast AGI threatens his **forecast role**; longer runways let him learn renewals and build direct client trust.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his forecast role before he gains enough client work to move.
whatWouldHelp: **Staffing dates**, client-data consent rules and real account vacancies would help him plan and speak plainly to analysts.
